# The upper threshold in ballistic annihilation

**Authors:** Debbie Burdinski Address: Debbie Burdinski Email address: debbie.burdinski@duke.edu , Shrey Gupta Address: Shrey Gupta Email address: shrey.gupta@duke.edu and Matthew Junge Address: Matthew Junge Email address: jungem@math.duke.edu

## Abstract

Three-speed ballistic annihilation starts with infinitely many particles on the real line. Each is independently assigned either speed- $0$ with probability $p$ , or speed- $\pm 1$ symmetrically with the remaining probability. All particles simultaneously begin moving at their assigned speeds and mutually annihilate upon colliding. Physicists conjecture when $p\leq p_{c}=1/4$ all particles are eventually annihilated. Dygert et. al. prove $p_{c}\leq.3313$ , while Sidoravicius and Tournier describe an approach to prove $p_{c}\leq.3281$ . For the variant in which particles start at the integers, we improve the bound to $.2870$ . A renewal property lets us equate survival of a particle to the survival of a Galton-Watson process whose offspring distribution a computer can rigorously approximate. This approach may help answer the nearly thirty-year old conjecture that $p_{c}>0$ .

## 1. Introduction

Two decades ago, physicists devoted considerable attention to a simple but difficult to analyze process called ballistic annihilation [EF85, CPY90, BF95, DRFP95, MP94, KRL95, Red97, Tri02]. Particles are placed on the real line according to a unit intensity Poisson point process and each is independently assigned a speed according to a probability measure $\nu$ . After this assignment, the model is deterministic; particles move at their speed and mutually annihilate upon colliding. The canonical example is with speeds from $\{-1,0,1\}$ sampled according to the symmetric measure

$$ \displaystyle\nu=\frac{1-p}{2}\delta_{-1}+p\delta_{0}+\frac{1-p}{2}\delta_{1}. $$

Physicists refer to this as an $A+A\to 0$ process. Ballistic annihilation was introduced in [EF85] with just two speeds. The goal was to study interactions of ideal gas particles. A few years later it was discussed in the context of arbitrary continuous $\nu$ [BNRL93]. The authors’ motivation was to understand “intriguing features” in the decay kinetics of irreversible aggregation, $A_{i}+A_{j}\to A_{i+j}$ , which has been used to model coalescence of fluid vortices [Mcw84] and planet formation by accretion [WD89]. The authors give heuristics for the decay rate of particles, and conjecture it responds continuously to perturbations in the speed measure.

The followup work [KRL95] predicts more interesting behavior in ballistic annihilation with discrete speeds. It is thought that the process undergoes an abrupt phase transition. Consider ballistic annihilation with the measure from (1). We will call speed- $0$ particles inert and speed- $\pm 1$ particles active. Let $\theta_{t}(p)$ be the probability an inert particle survives up to time $t$ , and $\theta(p)=\theta_{\infty}(p)$ be the probability it is never annihilated. Krapivsky et. al. infer in [KRL95] that there is a critical value $p_{c}$ such that $\theta(p)=0$ for $p\leq p_{c}$ , and above $p_{c}$ it holds that $\theta(p)>0$ . They conjecture $p_{c}=1/4$ and make precise predictions for the behavior of $\theta_{t}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{t}(p)\sim\begin{cases}C_{p}t^{-1},&p<p_{c}\\
Ct^{-2/3},&p=p_{c}\\
2-p^{-1/2},&p>p_{c}\end{cases},\qquad\text{ with }\qquad C_{p}=\frac{2p}{(1-4p)\pi}\text{ and }C=\frac{2^{2/3}}{4\Gamma(2/3)^{2}}. $$

A simple heuristic is given in [DRFP95] for why $p_{c}=1/4$ . Active particles move towards one another at relative speed 2, while the gap between a moving and inert particle is covered at relative speed 1. Thus, collisions between active particles ought to occur twice as often as those between inert and active particles. If we look at all of the collisions in a large interval, then each is one of three possibilities:

$$ \displaystyle(0,-1),(1,0),\text{ and }(1,-1). $$

Doubling the $(1,-1)$ -collisions to account for the prediction that these occur twice as often, we expect on average that for every eight particles removed, two are inert particles. So, when $p=1/4$ the collision types balance.

Symmetry ensures that active particles are annihilated almost surely (see [DJK+16, Proposition 16].) Note that [DRFP95] also provides a description of the decay density of $\pm 1$ -speed particles in the different regimes of $p$ . For $p<1/4$ the right tail is predicted to have exponent $-1/2$ . At criticality it is claimed to be $-1$ , and for $p>p_{c}$ they infer that the survival time decays at an exponential rate. Droz et. al. in [DRFP95] provide a nearly complete proof of these conjectures (including those for $\theta_{t}(p)$ predicted by [KRL95]). However, some steps are not rigorous and the argument gives little intuition. These formulas come from a complicated differential equation involving the distance between neighbor particles at time $t$ . Krapivsky et. al. point out in [KRL95] that there is still need for methods “that would provide better intuitive insights into the intriguing qualitative features of ballistic annihilation.” For example, there is no probabilistic proof that $p_{c}\neq 0$ , let alone is equal to $1/4$ .

As for upper bounds, Dygert et. al. prove that $p_{c}\leq.3313$ [DJK+16]. Additionally, [ST17] considers ballistic annihilation. Sidoravicius and Tournier prove that $p_{c}\leq 1/3$ , and outline an approach to prove $p_{c}\leq 0.3280$ . Their proof, like the one contained in this work, is recursive in nature. The configuration of particle speeds is revealed in blocks, and the number of surviving particles can be estimated by the subconfiguration in these blocks. The main difference is that we focus on the number of surviving inert particles at a special renewal time (?THM? ). This yields a necessary and sufficient condition for survival in terms of a Galton-Watson process (?THM? ). Moreover, because we consider unit-spacings between particles, it is more computationally tractable to estimate the offspring distribution of the Galton-Watson process (?THM? ). We are not trying to start a hunt for bounds closer and closer to the conjectured value. Rather, by improving the known bound, we reveal a new perspective into what promotes survival of speed-0 particles. Ideally this may help prove the central question in ballistic annihilation, that, for small $p$ , inert particles do not survive.

In this article, we consider ballistic annihilation with an inert particle at the origin, and particles placed on $\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ with i.i.d. speeds sampled according to $\nu$ from (1). To distinguish our case from ballistic annihilation with exponentially distributed spacings, we define $\psi(p)$ as the probability the speed-0 particle at the origin is never annihilated, and

$$ p^{\prime}_{c}=\inf\{p\colon\psi(p)>0\}. $$

Understanding survival of inert particles appears to be equally interesting and challenging whether the spacings are deterministic, or exponential(1) distributed. This is supported by recent findings [BM17] for the closely related bullet process with finitely many particles and a non-atomic probability measure on speeds. They find that the law for the number of surviving particles is independent of the initial spacings. Our main result is an improved bound for $p_{c}^{\prime}$ .

#### Theorem 1.

$p_{c}^{\prime}\leq 0.2870$ .

For ballistic annihilation with unit spacings, triple collisions may slightly change the critical threshold. Let $q=(1-p)/2$ , so that the probability three consecutive particles triple collide is $pq^{2}$ (i.e. a $(1,0,-1)$ configuration). This is $\approx.07$ when $p=1/4$ . With exponential spacings, the process loses one inert and one active particle whenever this configuration occurs. However, with the triple collision, an extra active particle is destroyed. The heuristic at (2) predicts that, after one time unit, the density of $0$ -particles is

$$ w=p-2pq+pq^{2}. $$

The $2pq$ term accounts for the configurations $(1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$ . We add $pq^{2}$ to prevent double counting triple collisions. Similarly, the density of active particles is

$$ z=2(q-q^{2}-pq). $$

The heuristic at (2) suggest we solve $w=\frac{1}{4}z$ , which yields $p\approx.2450.$ Accordingly, we conjecture that $p_{c}^{\prime}<.2450<p_{c}.$ We do not think that $p_{c}^{\prime}$ is much smaller than $.2450$ . The next spacing at which a triple collision can occur is $(1,\;\cdot\;,\;\cdot\;,0,\;\cdot\;,\;\cdot\;,-1)$ . Such configurations have probability described by a degree-7 polynomial in $p$ and $q$ , and so the contribution will be very small.

We prove this by relating survival in ballistic annihilation to survival of a Galton-Watson process. The idea is that there is a random index $\eta$ for which (i) when restricted to just particles in $[0,\eta]$ only inert particles survive, and (ii) the speeds of particles beyond $\eta$ are independent. If $Z$ is the number of surviving inert particles in the process restricted to $[0,\eta]$ , then (ii) guarantees that each of these particles will independently spawn $Z$ -distributed more surviving inert particles. Because each new generation is determined independently, we obtain a Galton-Watson process that counts surviving particles.

The construction of $\eta$ is described in the proof of ?THM? , and the equivalence of $\psi(p)>0$ to survival of the induced Galton-Watson process is contained in ?THM? . This characterization

$$ \displaystyle\psi(p)>0\iff\mathbf{E}Z>1 $$

is novel and could be useful for showing a non-survival regime for inert particles. Note that we suppress the $p$ -dependence in the expectation and write $\mathbf{E}Z$ in place of $\mathbf{E}_{p}Z$ . The same reasoning we use to obtain (3) can be applied to the usual ballistic annihilation with exponential spacings. Thus, a similar equivalence holds for $\theta(p)$ . In ?THM? , we briefly sketch how to adapt ?THM? to this setting.

Once we have the equivalence at (3), we turn our attention to lower bounding $\mathbf{E}Z$ . There are certain random times before $\eta$ at which we can stochastically lower bound $Z$ . We then use a computer to estimate these probabilities. This is completely rigorous, but requires too many calculations to be done by hand.

### Notation

Depending on how specific we need to be, we will refer to particles with speeds $\pm 1$ as either active or as $\pm 1$ -particles. Because it will correspond to the original parent in a Galton-Watson process, we refer to the inert particle at the origin as the seed. The randomness in ballistic annihilation is an initial vector $\mathbf{X}=(X_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty}$ with $X_{0}=0$ and the $X_{i}$ for $i\geq 1$ are i.i.d. with law $\nu$ from (1). These are the particle speeds.

Let $a_{i}$ denote the particle initially at $i$ . We will let $a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}$ mean that particles at $i$ and $j$ mutually annihilate. With discrete speeds and spacings, it is possible that three particles collide simultaneously. Denote this with $a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}\leftrightarrow a_{k}$ . We emphasize that writing $a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}$ does not preclude a third particle also being annihilated. That is $\{a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}\}\cap\{a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}\leftrightarrow a_{k}\}\neq\varnothing.$ We will sometimes use the more specific notation $a_{i}\mapsto a_{j}$ for when the active particle from $i$ annihilates the inert particle at $j$ .

## 2. An embedded Galton-Watson process

To show that inert particles survive with positive probability, it suffices to establish that the seed is never annihilated with positive probability. This is because an inert particle, say $a_{n}$ , has $n$ particles to its left, and thus has some positive probability of not being annihilated from that side. For example, all left particles are inert with probability $p^{n-1}$ . Conditional on surviving from the left, the probability that $n$ is never annihilated by a particle from the right is the same as the probability the seed survives. This follows via the coupling that aligns the speeds to the right of the seed with those to the right of $a_{n}$ in two independent processes.

That said, in this section, we develop a framework that lets us relate survival of the seed to non-extinction of a Galton-Watson process that counts surviving inert particles. This is made explicit in ?THM? . The construction hinges upon a renewal structure that has nice monotonicity properties. It rests upon the following two lemmas.

#### Lemma 2.

Let $i<j$ and $X_{j}=-1$ . The random variables $(X_{k})_{k>j}$ are $\nu$ -distributed and independent of the event $\{a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}\}$ .

#### Proof.

The particles to the right of $a_{j}$ cannot influence the event $\{a_{i}\leftrightarrow a_{j}\}$ , thus the speeds are independent of the event. ∎

If an active particle destroys an inert particle, then this induces a short range dependence. We know that all of the active particles that could reach the inert particle before its destroyer arrives must be annihilated. However, if we look sufficiently far away the particle speeds are once again independent.

#### Lemma 3.

Let $i<j$ and $X_{j}=0$ . The random variables $(X_{k})_{k>j+(j-i)}$ are independent of the event $\{a_{i}\mapsto a_{j}\}$ .

#### Proof.

It is elementary to work out that the particles beyond $j+(j-i)$ cannot reach $a_{j}$ before $a_{i}$ does, thus their speeds are independent of the event. ∎

#### Remark 4.

The speed $X_{j+(j-i)}$ is independent of $\{a_{i}\mapsto a_{j}\}$ but possibly $a_{j+(j-i)}$ triple collides with $a_{j}$ .

Conditioned on the event from ?THM? we will refer to $[i,2j-i]$ as a window of dependence. Given $\mathbf{x}=(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ , we define $\BA(\mathbf{x})$ to be ballistic annihilation on $\mathbb{R}$ with particles at $0,1,\ldots,n$ where the particle at $i$ has speed $x_{i}$ . Run $\BA(\mathbf{x})$ until every collision that could occur has occurred (this takes at most $n$ time units). Let

$$ \displaystyle\xi_{i}(\mathbf{x})=x_{i}\mathbf{1}{\{a_{i}\text{ survives}\}}+2\cdot\mathbf{1}{\{a_{i}\text{ is annihilated}\}} $$

and $\xi(\mathbf{x})=(\xi_{0},\ldots,\xi_{n})$ so that the $i$ th entry is the speed of $a_{i}$ if it survives, or $2$ if $a_{i}$ is annihilated in $\BA(\mathbf{x})$ .

We return to ballistic annihilation with the seed at the origin and a particle with a $\nu$ -distributed speed at each nonnegative integer. The last piece of notation we need is that $\mathbf{X}[i,j]=(X_{i},\ldots,X_{j})$ is the restriction to the coordinates between $i$ and $j$ . We now explain the renewal structure. The following proposition asserts that there exists a random index $\eta$ such that only inert particles survive in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])$ , and the particle speeds beyond $\eta$ are independent.

#### Proposition 5.

There exists a random variable $\eta\geq 1$ such that either

- (i) $\eta=\infty$ and the seed survives, or

- (ii) $\eta<\infty$ and $\xi(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])\subseteq\{0,2\}^{\eta}$ and $(X_{i})_{i>\eta}$ are $\nu$ -distributed and independent of $\eta$ and each other. Additionally, if $\eta>1$ , then the seed survives in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])$ .

#### Proof.

We remark that the last condition of (ii) for $\eta>1$ is included to exclude the trivial renewal time at the index of the $-1$ -particle that destroys the seed. So, unless $\eta=1$ , the particle at $\eta$ will not destroy the seed.

We define $\eta$ in terms of $X_{1}$ and a random variable $\eta_{1}$ for the distance we must look out for the process to be completely independent of how $a_{1}$ is annihilated when $X_{1}=1$ :

$$ \displaystyle\eta:=\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}\neq 1\}}+\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=1\}}\eta_{1}. $$

Now we describe $\eta_{1}$ . Consider ballistic annihilation with $X_{0}=0$ and $X_{1}=1$ , and let $\gamma_{1}$ be the index of the particle $a_{1}\leftrightarrow a_{\gamma_{1}}$ . First off, if $\gamma_{1}=\infty$ then set $\eta_{1}=\infty$ and the seed survives. Supposing $\gamma_{1}<\infty$ , if there is a triple collision, we take the larger of the two indices (so necessarily $X_{\gamma_{1}}=-1$ in this case). If $X_{\gamma_{1}}=-1$ , then we set $\eta_{1}=\gamma_{1}$ . In this case, we have $\xi(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta_{1}])=\{0\}\times\{2\}^{\eta_{1}}$ , and the particle speeds beyond $\eta_{1}$ are independent because of the renewal in ?THM? .

It gets more complicated when $X_{\gamma_{1}}=0$ . ?THM? with $i=1$ and $j=\gamma_{1}$ tells us that there is an $I_{1}:=[1,2\gamma_{1}-1]$ window of dependence on this event. Let $\mathbf{X}_{1}=\mathbf{X}[0,2\gamma_{1}-1]$ and

$$ \tau_{1}=\max\{i\in I_{1}\colon\xi_{i}(\mathbf{X}_{1})=0\} $$

be the starting location of the rightmost surviving inert particle. Note that the seed must survive, so we know that $\tau_{1}$ is well defined and nonnegative. Also, let

$$ \kappa_{1}=\min\{\tau_{1}\leq i\leq 2\gamma_{1}-1\colon\xi_{i}(\mathbf{X}_{1})=1\} $$

be the first surviving $1$ -particle to the right of $\tau_{1}$ . If there is no such particle, set $\kappa_{1}=0.$ We will consider this case separately in a moment.

If $\kappa_{1}>0$ , then we let $\gamma_{2}$ be such that $a_{\kappa_{1}}\leftrightarrow a_{\gamma_{2}}$ . In words, $\gamma_{2}$ is the index of the particle that destroys the active particle $a_{\kappa_{1}}$ . As before, if there is a triple collision, then we take the particle with larger index. If $X_{\gamma_{2}}=-1$ , then the process renews and we set $\eta_{1}=\gamma_{2}$ . If not, then a new window of dependence is induced by the event $\{a_{\kappa_{1}}\mapsto a_{\gamma_{2}}\}$ . We once again look at the furthest left surviving $1$ -particle and either set $\eta_{1}$ equal to the index of the $-1$ -particle that destroys it, or iterate another step if the particle hits an inert particle, causing a new window of dependence. This will either: halt eventually, giving some value of $\eta_{1}$ ; never halt, in which case $\eta_{1}=\infty$ ; or give some $\kappa_{i}=0$ , which puts us in the case described now for $\kappa_{1}$ .

If $\kappa_{1}=0$ , then there are no surviving active particles in $\BA(\mathbf{X}_{1})$ . However, it is possible that some $1$ -particles that annihilate inert particles in $\BA(\mathbf{X}_{1})$ will survive longer when particles from beyond $\mathbf{X}_{1}$ are introduced. For example, the survival of a $1$ -particle annihilated by an inert particle at $x$ is prolonged if a $-1$ -particle started outside of $\mathbf{X}_{1}$ reaches $x$ first. To account for this, we look at the collection of $1$ -particles from $\BA(\mathbf{X}_{1})$ that are destroyed by inert particles

$$ J=\{j\colon X_{j}\in\mathbf{X}_{1},X_{j}=1,a_{j}\mapsto a_{j^{\prime}}\text{ with }X_{j^{\prime}}=0\}. $$

If $J$ is empty, then we set $\eta_{1}=2\gamma_{1}-1$ . Otherwise, for each $j\in J$ we augment $\mathbf{X}_{1}$ to a larger interval $\mathbf{X}_{1,j}=\mathbf{X}[w_{j},z_{j}]$ defined to be the interval such that a $-1$ -particle at $z_{j}$ could triple collide (if it had a clear path) with $a_{j}$ and $a_{j^{\prime}}$ . Set $z=\max_{j\in J}z_{j}$ to be the furthest right index that we must consider in order to know whether each collision $a_{j}\mapsto a_{j^{\prime}}$ occurs in the $\BA(\mathbf{X})$ .

If all of the collisions counted by $J$ occur, then we possibly gain some additional particles in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,z])$ . However, since all of the collisions in $J$ still occurred we once again cannot have any surviving $-1$ -particles in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,z])$ . So, we repeat the procedure from some $\kappa_{2}$ equal to the leftmost surviving $1$ -particle in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,z])$ . This will either eventually terminate and we will obtain $\eta$ , or never halt and set $\eta=\infty$ with the seed never being reached by a $-1$ -particle.

The last case to consider is that some collision counted by $J$ does not occur because a particle from $[2\gamma_{2}-1,z]$ reaches an inert particle first. Letting $\kappa_{2}$ be the leftmost such $1$ -particle, we then know that $a_{\kappa_{2}}$ will now survive longer when we introduce more particles to the right. We set $\gamma_{2}$ to be the index such that $a_{\kappa_{2}}\leftrightarrow a_{\gamma_{2}}$ . This reinitiates the procedure we have defined, which will either terminate at a renewal time $\eta$ , or never terminate so that $\eta=\infty$ and the seed survives. ∎

#### Remark 6.

A similar statement also holds when particles are placed according to a unit intensity Poisson process. ?THM? and ?THM? still hold in this setting, and thus we can follow the same steps to obtain a renewal as in ?THM? .

Define the random variable $Z=|\{i\colon\xi_{i}(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])=0\}|$ to be the number of surviving inert particles. Because the process renews after $\eta$ we can link the expected number of surviving inert particles in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])$ to $\psi(p)$ via a Galton-Watson process.

#### Proposition 7.

Let $\eta$ be as in ?THM? and $Z\geq 0$ be the number of surviving inert particles from $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])$ . It holds that

$$ \psi(p)>0\iff\mathbf{E}Z>1. $$

#### Proof.

The random variable $Z$ can be used as the offspring distribution for a Galton-Watson process that counts surviving inert particles. Starting with the seed, ?THM? ensures that we have $Z$ inert particles in $[0,\eta]$ that survive from $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])$ . Moreover, the speeds $(X_{i})_{i>\eta}$ are i.i.d. $\nu$ -distributed.

We claim that each of these $Z$ particles will (eventually) serve as a seed that spawns $Z$ -distributed more surviving inert particles. We do this in a “depth first” manner. Consider the rightmost surviving inert particle in $[0,\eta]$ . Say it is at $i$ . By construction there are no surviving active particles in $[i,\eta]$ . If $i=\eta$ , then this is exactly the same initial configuration as with the seed. Even if $i<\eta$ , we still obtain a $Z$ -distributed number of surviving inert particles before the process renews. This is because a $-1$ -particle must destroy the inert particle at $i$ . This happens irregardless of whether or not there is a gap $(i<\eta)$ or not ( $i=\eta)$ . We continue generating $Z$ offspring at each surviving inert particle and stop if the process goes extinct.

The previous discussion implies that if the $Z$ -distributed Galton-Watson process survives then the seed is never annihilated. Conversely, if $\psi(p)>0$ , then the seed survives with positive probability. This can only happen if the Galton-Watson process started from the seed does not going extinct. The result follows from the elementary fact that non-extinction of a Galton-Watson process with positive probability is equivalent to $\mathbf{E}Z>1$ . ∎

## 3. Approximating $\mathbf{E}Z$

The complicated definition of $\eta$ from ?THM? suggests it would be difficult to calculate $\mathbf{E}Z$ explicitly. Even calculating the distribution of $\eta$ seems beyond our reach. However, there are certain times before $\eta$ at which we can obtain lower bounds on $\mathbf{E}Z$ . It helps to explain our approach in stages. First, we consider the effect of $a_{1}$ .

### 3.1. The effect of $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,1])$

The simplest lower bound on $Z$ is to look at what happens in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,1])$ . If $X_{1}=-1$ , then $Z=0$ , and if $X_{1}=0$ , then $Z=2$ . This gives

$$ \displaystyle Z\succeq\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=0\}}2. $$

Thus, if $p>1/2$ , we have $\mathbf{E}Z>1$ . Equivalently, $p_{c}^{\prime}\leq 1/2$ . This is a start, but not so interesting. The same statement could be proven by accounting for the number of inert particles versus active particles with a $p$ -biased random walk. Survival of the seed is equivalent to the walk never returning to 0, which happens with positive probability when $p>1/2$ .

Let us go one step further by considering the case $\eta>1$ . If $X_{1}=1$ , then the seed will not be annihilated by any particles in $[0,\eta]$ by construction of $\eta$ . Thus, $Z\succeq 1$ on this event. This gives the more meaningful bound

$$ \displaystyle Z\succeq\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=0\}}2+\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=1\}}. $$

Taking expectation in (7) yields $\mathbf{E}Z\geq 2p+\frac{1-p}{2}.$ When $p>1/3$ , this is larger than $1$ . Thus, we arrive easily at the bound $p_{c}^{\prime}\leq 1/3$ , which is proven in [DJK+16] and proven for $p_{c}$ in [ST17].

### 3.2. The effect of $a_{\gamma_{1}}$

We can do better by extracting some benefit from the $1$ -particle at $1$ . Let $\gamma_{1}$ be the index of the particle that destroys $a_{1}$ as in the proof of ?THM? . Let $Z_{1}$ be the number of surviving inert particles in the window of dependence induced by the event $\{a_{1}\leftrightarrow a_{\gamma_{1}}\}$ . Depending on whether $X_{\gamma_{1}}=-1$ or $0$ , this window is either $[0,\gamma_{1}]$ or $[0,2\gamma_{1}-1]$ . By construction, these inert particles will not be destroyed in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,\eta])$ , and thus $\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=1\}}Z_{1}\preceq\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=1\}}Z$ . This lets us improve (7) to the following dominance relation

$$ \displaystyle Z\succeq\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=0\}}2+\mathbf{1}{\{X_{1}=1\}}Z_{1}. $$

Figure 1 depicts a realization in which $Z_{1}=2$ .

*Figure 1. In this example, $\gamma_{1}=9$ . We are left with $Z_{1}=2$ surviving inert particles in $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,2\gamma_{1}-1])$ .*

To better understand $Z_{1}$ , we decompose it relative to the behavior of $\gamma_{1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle Z_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}{\{\gamma_{1}=n\}}Z_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}{\{X_{\gamma_{1}}=-1,\gamma_{1}=n\}}+\mathbf{1}{\{X_{\gamma_{1}}=0,\gamma_{1}=n\}}Z_{1} \displaystyle=1+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}{\{X_{\gamma_{1}}=0,\gamma_{1}=n\}}(Z_{1}-1). $$

Note that $\gamma_{1}\geq 2$ since we only introduce $\gamma_{1}$ when $X_{1}=1$ , and so the particle that destroys $a_{1}$ must start at $2$ or beyond. All of the cases where $X_{\gamma_{1}}=-1$ are included in the leading $1$ summand, so we devote our attention to when $X_{\gamma_{1}}=0$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}=\{X_{\gamma_{1}}=0,\gamma_{1}=n\}\subseteq\{0\}\times\{1\}\times\{-1,0,1\}^{2n-2} $$

be the set of sub-configurations for which $\gamma_{1}=n$ and $X_{\gamma_{1}}=0$ . Notice we only need to know the entries up to $2n-1$ to determine if $a_{1}\mapsto a_{n}$ .

In light of (9), we would like to understand $\mathbf{E}[\mathbf{1}{\{A_{n}\}}(Z_{1}-1)]$ . An important observation is that $Z_{1}-1\geq 0$ since the seed always survives in $\BA([0,2\gamma_{1}-1])$ . This means we can lower bound the expectation by computing its value for finitely many $n$ . We do so by counting surviving inert particles in the final state of $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,2\gamma_{1}-1])$ in each of the $3^{2n-2}$ possible realizations of particle speeds from $\{0\}\times\{1\}\times\{-1,0,1\}^{2n-2}$ .

Given $\mathbf{x}\in A_{n}$ , let $I(\mathbf{x})$ be the number of $0$ -entries in $\mathbf{x}$ . Simply by the definition of $\nu$ at (1), the probability $\mathbf{x}$ occurs is

$$ q_{n}(\mathbf{x}):=p^{I(\mathbf{x})}\left(\frac{1-p}{2}\right)^{2n-2-I(\mathbf{x})}. $$

Letting $Z_{1}(\mathbf{x})$ be the number of surviving inert particles in $\BA(\mathbf{x})$ , we then have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathbf{1}{\{A_{n}\}}(Z_{1}-1)]=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in A_{n}}q_{n}(\mathbf{x})[Z_{1}(\mathbf{x})-1]. $$

This is possible for a computer to calculate for small values of $n$ . For instance, if we compute for $n\leq 18$ (approximately 400 million cases) and take expectation in (9), we obtain the bound

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}Z_{1}\geq 1+\sum_{n=2}^{18}\sum_{x\in A_{n}}q_{n}(\mathbf{x})[Z_{1}(\mathbf{x})-1]=m(p), $$

and thus by (8) we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}Z\geq 2p+\frac{1-p}{2}m(p). $$

By numerically checking the boundary values of $p$ , we find that $\mathbf{E}Z>1$ when $p>0.2914$ . Note that $m(.2914)\approx 1.1178$ . So the “gain” we had from the previous calculation is $\approx.1178$ more expected surviving inert particles.

### 3.3. Using a surviving $1$ -particles from $\BA(\mathbf{X}[0,2\gamma_{1}-1])$

A simple way to optimize further is by re-using the previous calculation for configurations from $A_{n}$ in which there is a single surviving $1$ -particle at $2n-1$ , and otherwise only inert particles. Formally, let

$$ A_{n}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{x}\in A_{n}\colon\xi_{2n-1}(\mathbf{x})=1,\xi_{i}(\mathbf{x})\in\{0,2\}\text{ for }0\leq i\leq 2n-2\} $$

be the set of all such configurations. We claim that each $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in A_{n}^{\prime}$ provides an independent $Z_{1}-1$ distributed number of inert particles. This is because the particle speeds to the right of $a_{2\gamma_{1}-1}$ are independent. Thus, we can couple the number of surviving inert particles induced by $a_{2\gamma_{1}-1}$ to $Z_{1}-1$ . We subtract 1 so we do not double count the seed. Let $b(p)=\sum_{n=1}^{18}\sum_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in A^{\prime}_{n}}q_{n}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ be the probability of a configuration from $A_{n}^{\prime}$ . Each time this occurs we obtain an expected $m(p)-1$ more inert particles with $m(p)$ from (12). This will happen geometric( $b(p)$ )-distributed many times, which has expectation $b(p)/(1-b(p))$ . It follows that we can improve our bound from (13) to the following

$$ \mathbf{E}Z\geq 2p+\frac{1-p}{2}\left(m(p)+\frac{b(p)}{1-b(p)}(m(p)-1)\right). $$

It takes a computer about three hours to obtain an algebraic expression for $b(p)$ . After doing so, we find that $\mathbf{E}Z>1$ when $p>.2870.$ In this case we have $m(p)\approx 1.1713$ and $b(p)\approx.1226.$

### 3.4. Further benefit from surviving active particles

The bound we obtain on $p_{c}^{\prime}$ is as far as seemed reasonable to push our technique. More complicated calculations can be done where one considers the impact of other configurations of surviving $1$ -particles to the right of $\gamma_{1}$ . For example, one might consider the case that there is a single surviving $1$ -particle at $2\gamma_{1}-k$ with $k\geq 1$ (we only consider $k=1$ ). However, we found that the improvements to our bound were very small (about a $.004$ to our bound on $p_{c}$ ) did not justify the added complexity to the argument. It is our belief that the main benefit to estimating $\mathbf{E}Z$ would come out of extending our approach and looking out to distances $n>18$ . When $p=.2870$ we exactly compute $P(\gamma_{1}\leq 18)=.9018$ . So, we are missing about $1/10$ of the right tail, which ought to contain a significant number of surviving inert particles. However, without a clever insight, extending much further appears computationally intractable.

Abstract: The exchange of biological matter between bacterial cells drives adaptation and evolution. However, whether bacteria can exchange functional proteins remains unclear. Here, we show that antibiotic treatment induces vesicle-mediated horizontal protein transfer within and between bacterial species. By combining a genetic system in Escherichia coli to track transfer events with single-cell transcriptomic profiling, we found that antibiotics stimulate the differentiation of an isogenic bacterial population into distinct transient cell states: donor cells that activate a membrane stress response to release protein-containing vesicles, and recipient cells that suppress this response to take up vesicle contents. This antibiotic-induced protein exchange enables dormant persister cells to acquire proteins from active neighbors, enhancing survival and revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism by which bacteria withstand antibiotic treatment.

The horizontal exchange of biological material drives prokaryotic evolution and the spread of

antibiotic resistance (1). It also enables interspecies competition and commensalism in nutrient-

limited environments (2, 3). However, beyond proteins delivered by specialized secretion

systems (4-6), it remains unclear whether functional proteins can translocate from one bacterium

to another.

Bacterial membrane vesicles, which are lipid nanoparticles that can be derived from outer and

inner membranes, and which can contain membranous, periplasmic, and cytosolic contents (7,

8), have been proposed to mediate the exchange of biological material, including protein,

between bacteria (9, 10). The incubation of bacteria with vesicle-enriched samples, derived from

concentrated culture supernatant, has been associated with adaptive behaviors such as nutrient

uptake and horizontal gene transfer (HGT) (9, 11, 12). Furthermore, the velocity and diffusivity

of vesicles increase during antibiotic treatment (13), suggesting that certain stresses might

promote vesicle-mediated material exchange (9, 13). However, prior readouts of vesicle-

mediated exchange, such as changes in recipient viability or acquisition of donor resistance

genes, are indirect and nonspecific (9, 12, 14-18). These readouts can be influenced by other

particles, including bacteriophages, that can co-purify with pelleted vesicles (9, 19).

Additionally, no genetic regulators of vesicle-mediated exchange have been identified, casting

further doubt on whether the phenotypes observed in these studies are truly vesicle-mediated (9,

20). Therefore, a sensitive and trackable method is needed to study material exchange by

membrane vesicles.

## Discussion

Here, we identified vesicle-mediated horizontal protein transfer (HPT) as form of bacterial

material exchange that occurs within and between gram-negative species. Using Escherichia

coli, we showed that antibiotic stress activates this exchange by inducing two opposing cell

states within an isogenic population: donors that release protein-filled vesicles and recipients that

take up vesicle contents. These unidirectional transfer events arise from antibiotic-driven

regulatory program divergence. The Cre–loxP reporter system allowed us to visualize this

process and reveal how antibiotics orchestrate vesicle production, uptake, and intercellular

protein trafficking (Fig. 5J).

In donors, the activation of the Psp response promotes the production of HPT vesicles (Fig. 5J).

The Psp response was discovered during phage infection, but it has since been associated with

protection from a wide variety of perturbations that disrupt inner membrane integrity and proton

motive force (41, 60, 61). We show that in addition to Psp’s protective properties at the

intracellular level, it confers benefits at the intercellular level by enabling the sharing of vesicle

contents among a population. PspA, a member of the conserved ESCRT-III–like membrane

remodeling protein, relocates from the cytoplasm to the inner membrane upon Psp activation and

is detectable in transfer vesicles (39, 62). ESCRT-III proteins are known to promote vesicle

budding in eukaryotes (63). As pspA deletion alone does not significantly reduce HPT vesicle

production, while the deletion of all Psp genes does, other Psp proteins may be functionally

redundant to PspA during HPT vesicle production in E. coli (Fig. 3H). The enrichment in HPT

vesicles of Cre, PspA, and phosphatidylglycerol, which PspA is known to preferentially bind to

(45), suggests that vesicle contents are selectively packaged and released. Prior studies have

demonstrated that Gram-negative bacteria produce vesicles containing inner membrane and

cytoplasmic material, likely through membrane fragmentation and recircularization or

coordinated budding of both outer and inner membranes (64, 65). Local increases in

phosphatidylglycerol content along portions of donor cell membrane could act as binding sites

for PspA, and these sites eventually form transfer vesicles either through membrane budding or

fragmentation.

In recipients, suppression of the Psp response promotes vesicle uptake. This trade-off in

reduction of membrane stress protection in exchange for uptake suggests that vesicle acquisition

provides a survival benefit. Consistently, we found that Psp suppression and vesicle uptake are

linked to enhanced antibiotic persistence through increased HipA expression. Single-cell RNA-

seq revealed opposing hipA and ribosomal gene expression signatures in donors and recipients.

Together with the finding that elevated HipA suppresses donor transfer while promoting

recipient uptake, this indicates that HipA activity helps determine whether cells within an

isogenic population adopt donor or recipient states. As HipA is suppressed by physical

association with the HipB repressor (66), it is possible that spontaneous changes in intracellular

HipB levels can lead to bistable switching between the donor and recipient cell states.

Increased vesicle exposure prior to lethal antibiotic treatment enhances antibiotic persistence.

Uptake of key proteins, such as ribosomal components, metabolic enzymes, or DNA repair

factors, from active neighbors may help persisters endure proteome-damaging stress despite

reduced protein synthesis. Alternatively, vesicle-derived proteins or signaling molecules may

further reinforce dormancy in competent cells. Indeed, prior studies have found that quorum

sensing molecules can be packaged into vesicles in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (67). Strategies to

reduce antibiotic persistence may involve disrupting horizontal protein transfer or redirecting this

pathway to deliver toxic cargo to persister cells.

Although our study focuses on E. coli, the observation of cross-species transfer suggests that

protein exchange may be widespread in microbial communities. HPT could create protein-

sharing networks that enhance collective adaptability under stress or, alternatively, promote

interbacterial competition. Understanding the ecological and evolutionary roles of intra- and

interspecies protein transfer will provide new insight into how bacterial communities persist in

hostile environments.

## Materials and Methods

Bacterial strains and growth conditions

Escherichia coli MG1655 and Pseudomonas putida KT2440 were used for all experiments. Cultures were streaked onto LB plates supplemented with antibiotics when necessary for plasmid maintenance. Single colonies were picked and inoculated into 3 mL of LB-Lennox media. For E. coli donors, liquid culture was supplemented +/-0.2% arabinose for Cre induction and +/- ciprofloxacin to induce transfer. For P. putida donors, liquid culture was supplemented 40 µg/mL kanamycin for plasmid maintenance, 1000 ng/mL ATc for Cre induction, and +/- ciprofloxacin to induce transfer. For E. coli recipients, liquid culture was supplemented +/- ciprofloxacin to induce transfer. Cultures were grown at 37°C. The minimum antibiotic concentration (MAC) was identified separately for each strain (Supplementary Table 1).

Colony PCR

Individual colonies were picked off the plate and directly added to GoTaq® Hot Start Green Master Mix (Promega M512C) with the appropriate primers. Amplification was performed per manufacturer instructions and bands were analyzed using the Azure C200 Gel Imaging Workstation where appropriate.

Supernatant isolation

Donor culture was harvested at exactly 16 hrs post-inoculation. Cells were pelleted in 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes, and 3 mL of supernatant was extracted and filtered by a 0.2 µm surfactant-free cellulose acetate filter (Corning 431219).

Donor-recipient cell and supernatant co-incubations

Cultures were grown as previously described and harvested at exactly 16 hours post-inoculation. To determine the frequency of cell-cell transfer, 500 uL of donor culture was combined with 500 uL of recipient culture, resuspended in 100 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose, and incubated for 1 hr at 37°C. For multi-hour cell-cell co-incubations in sublethal or lethal antibiotics, 250 uL of donor culture was combined with 250 uL of recipient culture and resuspended in 500 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose with the appropriate concentration of antibiotics. For cell-protein co-incubations, 500 uL of recipient culture was resuspended in 100 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose and purified Cre recombinase (NEB M0298L) was added. Samples were then incubated for up to 24 hours at 37°C. To determine the frequency of supernatant-cell transfer, 500 uL of recipient culture was resuspended in 100 uL of donor supernatant and incubated for 1 hr at 37°C. After co-incubations, mixtures were washed and resuspended in 500 uL of 1x MinA media + 1 mM MgSO4. Gal+ quantification was assessed by plating co-incubation mixtures onto 1x MinA plates supplemented with + 1 mM MgSO4 and 0.2% galactose at 37°C. Sodium dodecyl sulfate, nonylphenyl etheoxylate, loxP plasmid DNA, or Pronase was spiked into cell-cell or cellsupernatant co-incubation mixtures where applicable. Donor supernatant was pre-treated at 37°C for an hour with Pronase prior to co-incubation with recipients where applicable. All experiments were replicated a minimum of three times in the laboratory.

DNA co-incubation and electroporation

Donor genomic DNA was isolated from donor cultures with the Wizard® Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega A1120). 125 ng/uL of genomic DNA was fragmented for 3 hrs at 37°C with Fastdigest EcoRI (Thermo Scientific™ FD0274), then heat-inactivated at 80°C. Amplicons of the cre locus were prepared by performing colony PCR with Phusion Hot Start II DNA Polymerase (Thermo Scientific™ F549L) using primers located upstream and downstream of the cre gene as recorded in Supplementary Table 2. Genomic and amplicon samples were purified with the QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen 28104). AraC+ recipient culture was grown as previously described and harvested at 16 hrs post-inoculation. 10 uL of fragmented DNA or 100 ng of cre locus amplicon was co-incubated with 500 uL of recipient culture resuspended in 100 uL of LB + 0.2% arabinose for 1 hr at 37°C. The mixture was then resuspended and plated as described before for other co-incubations. For electroporation, AraC+ recipient culture was grown as previously described and harvested at 16 hrs post-inoculation, then diluted 1:100 in 100 mL of LB + 0.2% arabinose. Cultures were grown at 37°C until OD600 reached 0.4, then washed 3x with ice-chilled water before being resuspended in 1 mL of water. 50 uL of electrocompetent cells were electroporated with 2 uL of fragmented genomic DNA or 50 ng of cre locus amplicon using the BioRad Gene Pulser® II set to 1.4 kV. Cells were recovered in 1 mL LB-Lennox media for 1 hr at 37°C, diluted as necessary, and plated onto LB media for titers and 1.5% agar 1x MinA plates supplemented with 0.2% galactose + 1 mM MgSO4 for quantification of Gal+ frequency. All experiments were replicated a minimum of three times in the laboratory.

Western blotting and mass spectrometry

Cultures were grown as previously described. Protein was precipitated with 10% trichloroacetic acid and 0.015% sodium deoxycholate where necessary for samples with low protein concentrations. Protein pellets were resuspended in 100 uL of 2x Laemmli buffer with 1% betamercaptoethanol and neutralized with Tris-HCl. 10 uL of each sample were loaded into 10% Mini-PROTEAN® TGX™ Precast Protein Gels (BioRad 4561035) and run at 200V for 40 min. Lanes were transferred onto PVDF membranes using the Trans-Blot Turbo Mini 0.2 µm PVDF Transfer Packs (BioRad 1704156) and Trans-Blot Turbo Transfer System following the mixed molecular weight protocol. Membranes were blocked in 2% milk TBS-Tween 0.2% overnight at 4°C. Primary antibody was added to the blocking buffer (1:5,000 dilution for Cre recombinase Polyclonal Antibody, Invitrogen PA5-32244; 1:10,000 dilution for in-house rabbit polyclonal GroEL antibody) and incubated overnight at 4°C. Blots were washed 3x 5 min with TBS-Tween 0.2% at room temperature, then the secondary antibody was added (1:10,000 dilution, Goat antirabbit polyclonal Cy5, Invitrogen A10523) and incubated at room temperature for 1 hr, then washed 3x 5 min with TBS-Tween 0.2% and resuspended in TBS. Fluorescence signal was detected using the Azure C400 Gel Imaging system. Quantification of western blots was performed using FIJI (68) image processing package. For mass spectrometry, protein pellets were washed twice with 200 uL ice-cold acetone and air-dried for 10 min. Samples were submitted to the Baylor College of Medicine mass spectrometry core (RRID:SCR_027015) for analysis. Intensity based absolute quantification (iBAQ) was used to quantify protein abundance. Hierarchical protein clustering based on fraction of total protein abundance normalized separately across F2-F6 and across Cells and Sup was performed using the default settings of ComplexHeatmap v2.16.0 in R. Proteins absent from >1 replicate in each fraction or from >2 fractions were excluded from clustering.

Lipid extraction and analysis

Vesicle fractions (~1 mL) were mixed with 1 mL methanol and 2 mL chloroform, vortexed and incubated on nutating shaker for 15 mins. Extraction mixture was centrifuged at 1000 g for 10 mins. Bottom organic layer was collected. Top aqueous layer was acidified with 20 mL formic acid and re-extracted with 2 mL chloroform. Bottom organic layer from both steps were pooled and dried under N2 stream. Dried lipids were re-suspended in 50 mL 2:1 chloroform: methanol, 10 mL was injected on SHIMADZU Nexera UHPLC coupled with SCIEX ZenoTOF 7600 mass spectrometer. Chromatographic separation was achieved on C18 reverse phase column (Pheneomenex, 5 μm, 50 x 4.6 mm #00B-4435-E0). Solvent = 60:40 (v/v) ACN/water + 0.1% (v/v) formic acid + 10 mM ammonium formate, Solvent B = 90:10 (v/v) IPA: ACN + 0.1% (v/v) formic acid + 10 mM ammonium formate. Separation gradient started with 10% B for 0.5 mins, followed by a linear increase to 100% B from 0.5 to 25 mins, 100% B maintained at 28 mins, 10% B at 28.01 mins, 10% B maintained till 30 mins. Column temperature was maintained at 600C, and flow rate was maintained at 0.5 mL/min throughout the separation. ZenoTOF parameters were as follows: curtain gas = 45, CAD gas = 9, ion Source gas 1 = 40 psi, ion source gas 2 = 70 psi, temperature = 450 0C, spray voltage = -4500 V for negative mode and 5500 V for positive mode. TOF start mass = 200 Da, TOF stop mass = 2000 Da, accumulation time = 0.1 s, delustering potential = -40 V for negative mode and 40 V for positive mode, collision energy = - 12 V for negative mode and 12 V for positive mode, QJect RF amplitude = 193.78 V. MS/MS was acquired with CID fragmentation, TOF start mass = 100 Da, TOF stop mass = 2000 Da, accumulation time = 0.005 seconds, collision energy = -60V for negative mode and 60 V for positive mode with collision energy spread of 20 V, QJect RF amplitude = 202.72 V. Raw files were analyzed with MS-DIAL4.90, with  following parameters: MS1 tolerance = 0.01 Da, MS2 tolerance = 0.025 Da, peak detection = 1000 amplitude, mass slice width = 0.1 Da, MS2 deconvolution: sigma window value = 0.5, ms/ms abundance cutoff=0, ms/ms identification score cutoff = 80%. For alignment, retention time tolerance = 0.05 mins and MS1 tolerance = 0.015 Da. Lipids with no tandem mass fragment were removed. Area under the curve was used for quantitation. PG and Cardiolipin were analyzed in negative mode and PE were analyzed in positive mode. Lipid extraction and analysis were performed once with three independent biological replicates. Hierarchical clustering of lipid species by the relative abundance of each species normalized to total lipid in each fraction was performed using the default settings of ComplexHeatmap v2.16.0 in R.

RT-qPCR and bulk RNA sequencing Cultures were grown as previously described. Total RNA was harvested using the RNASnapTM protocol (69). RNA Clean & Concentrator Kit (Zymo Research) with on-column DNAse I digestion was performed and samples were resuspended in nuclease-free water. For RT-qPCR, 2 µg of total RNA were reverse transcribed using random hexamer primers (Thermo Scientific™ SO142) and SuperScript™ III Reverse Transcriptase (InvitrogenTM 18080093) per manufacturer’s instructions. PowerUp™ SYBR™ Green Master Mix (Applied BiosystemsTM A25742) with Cre and GroEL control primers were used to amplify samples on the QuantStudio 3 RT-PCR system. For RNA sequencing, 1 µg of total RNA was rRNA-depleted and prepared for sequencing with the NEBNext rRNA Depletion Kit (Bacteria) (NEB #E7850) and NEBNextUltra II RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB #E7770) per manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were multiplexed with NEBNext® Multiplex Oligos for Illumina® (NEB #E7600S). Paired-end sequencing was performed using the NextSeq 500/550 High Output Kit v2.5 75 cycles kit (NextSeq 20024906) on the Illumina NextSeq 550 system. Illumina reads were

Membrane vesicle purification and density gradient ultracentrifugation

Cultures were grown as previously described and donor supernatant was extracted. 4.8 mL of donor supernatant was added to Open-Top Thinwall Ultra-Clear tubes (5 mL, Beckman Coulter 344057). Vesicles were concentrated by pelleting at 300,000g x 5 hrs at 4°C with the SW55 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter 342196) and the Beckman Coulter Optima L-100K ultracentrifuge. Pelleted vesicles were resuspended in 300 uL of LB. For density gradient ultracentrifugation, concentrated vesicles were combined with OptiPrep™ Density Gradient Medium (Sigma- Aldrich D1556) for a final concentration of 45% OptiPrep, and 800 uL was loaded at the bottom of a 5 mL Ultra-Clear tube. 800 uL each of 40%, 35%, 30%, 25%, and 20% Optiprep diluted in 1x PBS were overlayed sequentially on top of the layer of concentrated vesicles. Ultracentrifugation was performed at 200,000g x 21 hrs using the same rotor and ultracentrifuge as before. 400 uL layers were extracted top to bottom, discarding the first and last layer, for a total of 10 layers. To solubilize membranes, pelleted vesicles were treated at 37°C for 1 hour with 1% SDS prior to SDS precipitation by KCl and density gradient ultracentrifugation. Density gradient layers were co-incubated with recipients or prepared for western blotting as previously described. For nano flow cytometry and structured illumination microscopy of concentrated supernatant, 50 mL of supernatant for each sample was centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 30 min at 4° C. The supernatants were transferred to new microfuge tubes and filtered using 0.22 μm filter units. Vesicles were collected by ultracentrifugation (type 45Ti rotor, Optima L-80 XP Ultracentrifuge Beckman Coulter) at 41000 rpm for 16 h at 4° C. Pellets containing isolated vesicles were resuspended in 500 ml PBS 1X (filtered using 0.02 μm filter units) and stored at 4° C. All fractions of isolated vesicles were verified by fluorescence microscopy (using the FM4-64 membrane dye (Thermofisher scientific # T13320)). All experiments were replicated a minimum of three times in the laboratory.

Cryo-electron tomography

Density gradient samples were mixed with 10 nm diameter colloidal gold beads (used as fiducial markers in image alignment) and deposited onto freshly glow-discharged, lacey carbon film grids for 1 min. The grids were then blotted with filter paper and rapidly frozen in liquid ethane, using a gravity-driven plunger apparatus. Frozen-hydrated specimens were imaged using a 200 keV Thermo Scientific Glacios® Cryo-Transmission Electron Microscope equipped with Falcon 4i Direct Electron Detector. The microscope was operated at 200 kV with a magnification of ×49,000, resulting in an effective pixel size of 2.56 Å at the specimen level. We used software TOMO to collect low-dose, single-axis tilt series with dose fractionation mode at about 6 µm defocus. Tilt series were collected from -51° to 51° with increment of 3° and a cumulative dose of ~80 e− /Å2 distributed over 35 stacks. Each stack contains ~7 images. We used IMOD to facilitate data processing, which includes drift correction of dose-fractionated data and assembly of corrected sums into tilt series, automatic fiducial seed model generation, alignment and

<!-- Page 42 -->


contrast transfer function correction of tilt series, and weighted back projection (WBP) reconstruction of tilt series into tomograms. Each tomographic reconstruction is 1,024 × 1,024 × 300 pixels in pixel size of 10.24 Å. In total, 5 tomographic reconstructions were made from F2 and F3 DG-UC fractions. Imaging was performed on two independent biological replicates simultaneously.

Cryogenic Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy (cryo-CLEM) and Cryogenic Electron Tomography (Cryo-ET) on Cre-mVenus-positive vesicles

F2-F3 (after density gradient ultracentrifugation) and P1 fractions were prepared from CremVenus+ cultures. They were then frozen, shipped overnight on dry ice, and stored at -80 °C in preparation for cryo-CLEM analysis. The sample was subsequently thawed once and vitrified on EM grids as previously described (74) using a Leica EM GP2 plunger freezer. Briefly, 4 μL of suspended vesicles were mixed with 10 nm gold fiducials and loaded onto glow-discharged EM grids (R2/2 Quantifoil Carbon membrane on a Cu 300 mesh). Grids were back blotted and plunged into liquid ethane/propane mixture maintained at -188 °C. Grids were then clipped into the autogrid setup and kept vitreous throughout the various imaging steps and storage. Cryo-LM imaging of mVenus signal was performed as z-stacks using 3.6% of 488 nm laser and a GaAsP- PMT detector on a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss Inc., Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with a Linkam CMS196v3 cryostage (Linkam Scientific Instruments Ltd., Redhill, United Kingdom). The lower laser power ensured that the sample remained vitreous during imaging. A 100x air objective with an NA of 0.75 was used for imaging, resulting in a point spread function (PSF) of ~430 nm for mVenus signal (emission wavelength of mVenus is ~527 nm); lateral resolution (XY) by Rayleigh criterion = Nau x 0.61 x l / NA, where Nau is the pin hole size in Airy unit and l is the emission wavelength. Fluorescence targets were evaluated for the presence of mVenus signal by comparing their total intensity to that of the background. The focal plane for each of the targets was chosen out of the z-stack for this calculation. SNR was also calculated for each of the targets; SNR = (Mean target signal - mean background signal) / standard deviation of background signal. Cryo-EM and cryo-ET imaging was performed on a ThermoFisher Krios G3i equipped with a cold stage and a 300 keV field emission gun. Images were acquired using SerialEM software (76) on a K3 direct electron detector (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, CA, USA) operated in the electron-counted mode. Gatan Imaging Filter (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, CA, USA) with a range of slit widths (20 – 100 eV) was used to increase contrast at various magnifications. The workflow for cryo-CLEM and cryo-ET is as follows. We first assessed the sample by cryo-EM using magnifications ranging for 82 X, all the way up to 19500 X – we took caution to keep electron radiation damage to negligibly low levels during this initial cryo-EM screening. We then imaged the sample by cryo-LM to assess the distribution of mVenus signal and to identify fluorescent foci that are likely compatible with cryo-EM imaging based on our previous assessments. The sample was re-imaged by cryo-EM to locate the same fluorescent signals. Correlations were performed within SerialEM to sufficient accuracy that ensured capturing the target of interest within the field of view, even at the highest magnification of interest (corresponding to correlation accuracy of 500 nm or better). Single-cell transcriptomics

Donors and loxP-mScarlet recipients were co-incubated at a cfu ratio of 1:10 as previously described. After co-incubation, cells were recovered for one hour in MinA media supplemented with 0.2% glucose and 1 mM MgSO4. Bacteria were harvested and scRNA-seq was performed using the smRandom-seq technology (78) without running the Cas9-based step for the depletion of ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-derived amplified and barcoded cDNA. Briefly, DNA primers were conjugated to hydrogel beads and then barcoded using a 3-round, split-pool ligation, allowing a total barcode multiplicity of 96 x 48 x 48, with the UMI and dT tail added on the last round of ligation. Cells were fixed, permeabilized, and quantified, and two technical replicates were pooled. In-situ reverse transcription and dA tailing were performed. Cells, barcoding buffer, barcoded beads, and a continuous oil phase were flowed through the respective channels of a cell and bead encapsulation device (79). Droplets encapsulating cells and beads were collected and thermocycled to barcode cells. Droplet emulsions were broken to harvest barcoded cDNA, the sequencing library was prepared using TruSeq chemistry, and 150 bp paired-end sequencing was performed using Illumina’s NovaSeq X platform. Reads were quality-checked, trimmed, and binned according to unique cell barcodes. Reads were aligned to the Escherichia coli MG1655 genome appended with cre, mScarlet, and msGFP2 sequences. In total, 16k cells were included for downstream analysis. sctransform v2 (80) was used to normalize read counts and cells were clustered at 0.15 resolution using the Leiden clustering algorithm. Marker genes were defined as genes that were most distinctively overexpressed in each cluster relative to all other cells using using the scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups function. Normalized UMI counts were used to visualize data. Extraction and amplification was performed once on two independent biological replicates that were pooled prior to data analysis. Data in Fig. 4D was displayed as a UMAP projection with Leiden clustering of single cell transcriptomes. All code is archived and available in an online repository (81).
